q: Which transmission operators must put the automatic-activation frequency reserve energy platform into operation, and how long after approval of the implementation framework?
answer: All TSOs performing the automatic frequency restoration process under Part IV of Regulation (EU) 2017/1485 must implement and operate the platform for exchanging balancing energy from frequency restoration reserves with automatic activation by thirty months from approval of the implementation framework (or 12 months after approval of a modification proposal), and use it to submit and exchange all standard-product bids.

q: How long after the implementation framework is approved must the replacement-reserve energy exchange platform be operational, and which operators does that cover?
answer: One year after approval of the implementation framework. It covers all TSOs performing the reserve replacement process under Part IV of Regulation (EU) 2017/1485 that have at least one interconnected neighbouring TSO performing the replacement reserves process.

q: For which synchronous area must the pan-European imbalance netting platform be used as a minimum?
answer: TSOs performing the automatic frequency restoration process must use the imbalance netting platform to perform the imbalance netting process “at least for the Continental Europe synchronous area”, one year after approval of the implementation framework.

q: After the framework for the manual-activation reserve energy platform has been approved, may TSOs still propose changes to the platform, and what must support such a proposal?
answer: Yes: by eighteen months after approval of the implementation framework all TSOs may develop a proposal to modify the platform; the modification must be supported by a cost-benefit analysis performed by all TSOs under Article 61, and the proposal is notified to the Commission.

q: Which functions must the platform for netting imbalances consist of at minimum?
answer: At least the imbalance netting process function and the TSO-TSO settlement function, built on common governance principles and business processes and applying a multilateral TSO-TSO model.

q: When a regulator lets a transmission operator run energy storage under a derogation, does anyone at EU level have to be told about that decision?
answer: Yes. The decision to grant the derogation must be notified to the Commission and ACER together with relevant information about the request and the reasons for granting it.

q: How quickly must a distribution operator wind down its storage activities once a public consultation shows outside parties can run storage cost-effectively?
answer: Within 18 months: the regulatory authority must ensure the DSO's storage activities are phased out within 18 months, and may allow the DSO reasonable compensation, in particular to recover the residual value of its investment. The consultation is held at regular intervals or at least every five years.

q: Up to which year must the final investment decision on a battery have been taken for a transmission operator to keep it for the usual depreciation period despite the phase-out rule?
answer: Until 2024: the phase-out in paragraph 4 does not apply for the usual depreciation period of new battery storage facilities with a final investment decision until 2024, provided they are connected within two years, integrated in the transmission system, used only for reactive instantaneous restoration of network security and not used to buy or sell electricity, including balancing.

q: On what conditions may Member States allow distribution grid operators to run charging points for electric vehicles?
answer: Only by derogation, if all of the following hold: (a) other parties, after an open, transparent and non-discriminatory tender reviewed by the regulator, were not awarded the right or could not deliver at reasonable cost and in time; (b) the regulator has done an ex ante review of the tender conditions and approved; (c) the DSO operates the points on third-party access terms and does not discriminate between system users, in particular in favour of its related undertakings.

q: By when must TSOs draw up the proposal for sharing income from forward capacity allocation, and which earlier methodology must they take into account?
answer: Within six months after approval of the congestion-income sharing methodology referred to in Article 9(6) of Regulation (EU) 2015/1222, all TSOs jointly develop the forward-allocation methodology, taking into account the methodology developed under Article 73 of Regulation (EU) 2015/1222, whose requirements also apply.

q: By what date each year must national regulators inform ACER and publish a report on how scarcity income from interconnectors was used?
answer: By 1 March each year the regulatory authorities inform ACER and publish a report covering the revenue collected in the 12 months ending 31 December of the previous year, how it was used (including specific projects and the amount placed on a separate account line), the amount used in calculating network tariffs, and verification that this complies with the Regulation and the methodology.

q: Under the day-ahead and intraday capacity allocation and congestion management regulation (2015/1222), what must the methodology for sharing congestion income provide for when interconnector assets belong to someone other than a transmission operator?
answer: It must establish arrangements to share congestion income deriving from transmission assets owned by parties other than TSOs (Article 73(2)(e)).
review_note: Question scoped to Regulation 2015/1222. Regulation 2016/1719 Art 57(3) applies Art 73's requirements by reference, so the unscoped wording could also fit Art 57, which does not itself state the content.

q: If long-term transmission rights are curtailed before the day-ahead firmness deadline to stay within security limits, how are their holders compensated?
answer: The TSOs concerned on the bidding zone border compensate the holders of the curtailed long-term transmission rights with the market spread; the TSOs must also report the curtailment to the regulators and publish the reasons.
review_note: Provenance extended with paragraph 1: the answer's reporting/publication duty comes from Art 53(1), not 53(2).

q: A TSO invokes force majeure and cuts long-term transmission rights. What do the holders of those rights receive?
answer: Compensation from the TSO that invoked force majeure, for the period of the force majeure, equal to the amount initially paid for the long-term transmission right in the forward allocation process.

q: Who assesses whether an event counts as force majeure for curtailing allocated cross-border capacity, and under what condition does that role exist?
answer: Where a Member State has so provided, the national regulatory authority assesses, upon request by the TSO concerned, whether an event qualifies as force majeure. The same wording appears in Article 72(5) of Regulation (EU) 2015/1222 and Article 56(5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/1719.

q: After the day-ahead firmness deadline has passed, what may be done with cross-border capacity that was not allocated?
answer: It may be adjusted for subsequent allocations (Article 70(3)).

q: Over what kind of links must frequency restoration reserve activation between load-frequency control areas of different synchronous areas be carried out?
answer: Over HVDC interconnectors: TSOs implement frequency restoration power interchange between LFC areas of different synchronous areas by adjusting the active power flows over HVDC interconnectors (Art 147(5)); the HVDC operator controls the flow on the instructions of the reserve connecting or reserve receiving TSO (Art 176(4)).
review_note: Original wording ('reserve power ... different synchronous areas') fit both Art 147(5) (FRR) and Art 146(5) (imbalance netting power interchange), which has the same HVDC sentence. Question now names frequency restoration reserve. Added Art 176(4) (HVDC operators control the flow for FRR exchange between synchronous areas) as a second supporting article.

q: Which synchronous areas may ask not to run an automatic frequency restoration process, and how often must a granted exemption be revisited?
answer: The TSOs of the GB and IE/NI synchronous areas may each submit, within two years of entry into force, a proposal with a cost-benefit analysis showing higher costs than benefits; if approved, the TSOs and regulators must re-evaluate the decision at least every 4 years.

q: How is the area control error of a load-frequency control area computed?
answer: The ACE is the K-Factor of the LFC area multiplied by the frequency deviation, minus the total interconnector and virtual tie-line active power flow and minus the control program (Article 136).

q: On what ground may a TSO taking part in reserve sharing refuse to share?
answer: Any control capability providing, receiving or affected TSO may refuse sharing of FRR/RR where it would result in power flows that violate the operational security limits when the shared reserve capacity is activated.

q: When a load-frequency control block gets part of its required frequency restoration reserve from a block in another synchronous area, must the provider hold extra reserve capacity for that?
answer: Yes. The share is provided from the second synchronous area's LFC block in addition to the total reserve capacity on FRR that this second block itself requires under Article 157(1).

q: Until how long before the start of the delivery day must a service provider be allowed to pass its reserve capacity obligation to another provider?
answer: The transfer of balancing capacity must be allowed at least until one hour before the start of the delivery day, subject to the receiving provider being qualified, no endangering of operational security and no breach of operational limits.

q: By when must every cross-border exchange of balancing capacity follow the TSO-TSO model, and is there any exception?
answer: By four years after entry into force of the Regulation all exchanges of balancing capacity must be based on the TSO-TSO model; the requirement does not apply to the TSO-BSP model for replacement reserves if one of the two TSOs involved does not operate the reserve replacement process as part of the load-frequency-control structure.

q: Is a TSO allowed to enlarge its reliability margin because of exchanging reserve capacity with neighbours?
answer: No. TSOs shall not increase the reliability margin calculated under Regulation (EU) 2015/1222 due to the exchange of balancing capacity for frequency restoration reserves and replacement reserves (Regulation 2017/2195 Art 33(7)); Regulation (EU) 2019/943 Art 17(5) repeats the rule for the exchange of balancing capacity or sharing of reserves.
review_note: Regulation 2019/943 Art 17(5) states the same prohibition (exchange of balancing capacity or sharing of reserves), so it independently answers the question. Added to relevant ids and provenance; answer extended; type set to cross-act.

q: Under the electricity balancing guideline (Regulation 2017/2195), how long must the imbalance settlement period be, what is the deadline for applying it (counted from entry into force), and which operators may jointly request an exemption?
answer: 15 minutes, applied by all TSOs in all scheduling areas within three years of entry into force, with market time unit boundaries coinciding with the settlement period boundaries. The TSOs of a synchronous area may jointly request an exemption; where one is granted, regulators with the Agency must review it in a cost-benefit analysis at least every three years.
review_note: Unscoped, the question also fits Regulation 2019/943 Art 8(4), which sets a different regime (15 min by 1 Jan 2021, derogations to end-2024, 30 min from 2025) and does not say who may request an exemption. Question now scoped to the balancing guideline with the deadline counted from entry into force, so only Art 53 answers it.

q: How far into the future must the infrastructure scenarios reach when alternative bidding zone layouts are compared in a review?
answer: A bidding zone review must include scenarios covering a range of likely infrastructure developments throughout a period of 10 years starting from the year following the year in which the decision to launch the review was taken.

q: How often must each coordinated capacity calculator report the reductions that TSOs made when validating cross-zonal capacity, and to whom?
answer: Every three months each coordinated capacity calculator reports all reductions made during validation to all regulatory authorities of the capacity calculation region, stating the location and amount of each reduction and the reasons; the regulators decide whether to publish all or part of the report.
review_note: 'Units computing cross-border capacity' could be read as the regional coordination centres of Regulation 2019/943 Art 16(3), which also report every three months, but to regulators and ACER on coordinated reductions/deviations. Question now refers to reductions TSOs made during validation, matching Art 26(3)/(5).

q: Above what level of fossil CO2 emissions per kilowatt-hour may new power plants no longer be paid under a capacity mechanism?
answer: More than 550 g of CO2 of fossil fuel origin per kWh of electricity: generation capacity that started commercial production on or after 4 July 2019 may not be committed or receive payments under a capacity mechanism. Older plants are excluded from 1 July 2025 if they exceed both 550 g/kWh and 350 kg CO2 per installed kWe per year.

q: Can a household with its own battery be charged network fees twice for electricity it stores on its own premises?
answer: No. Active customers that own an energy storage facility must not be subject to double charges, including network charges, for stored electricity remaining within their premises or when providing flexibility services to system operators.
